title: Verify the Claim: Option A
text:
Part 1 — Reconstruct
The article compares the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 American Community Survey (ACS) five-year estimates. I use B17001_002 for the estimated number of people below the poverty level and B17001_001 for the population whose poverty status was determined. Dividing the first estimate by the second gives a poverty rate. I use ACS five-year data because those are the periods identified in the article and because tract-level data are available. The periods do not overlap: one ends in 2010 and the other begins in 2013.
The article reports figures for neighborhoods such as Eastwick and Fairhill but does not identify which census tracts it assigned to each neighborhood. I therefore analyze Philadelphia census tracts. I assume the same ACS poverty definition can be used in both periods. My tract results describe geographic patterns in the city; they cannot reproduce the article’s exact neighborhood estimates.


Show code
poverty_vars <- c(
  total = "B17001_001",
  below = "B17001_002"
)

get_poverty <- function(yr) {
  get_acs(
    geography = "tract",
    variables = poverty_vars,
    state = "PA",
    county = "Philadelphia",
    year = yr,
    survey = "acs5",
    output = "wide"
  ) %>%
    mutate(period = paste0(yr - 4, "-", yr))
}

poverty_2010 <- get_poverty(2010)
poverty_2017 <- get_poverty(2017)

title: Verify the Claim: Option A
text:
Part 2 — Test
For each tract, I calculate the poverty rate and use moe_prop() to calculate the margin of error (MOE) of that rate. The MOE of the poverty count cannot simply be used as the MOE of the rate. I then calculate the coefficient of variation (CV) from the rate’s standard error. I classify CV values below 12% as reliable, 12%–40% as somewhat reliable, and above 40% as unreliable.


Show code
calculate_rate <- function(data) {
  data %>%
    mutate(
      rate = case_when(
        totalE > 0 ~ belowE / totalE,
        TRUE ~ NA_real_
      ),
      rate_moe = case_when(
        totalE > 0 ~ moe_prop(belowE, totalE, belowM, totalM),
        TRUE ~ NA_real_
      ),
      cv = case_when(
        rate > 0 ~ (rate_moe / 1.645) / rate * 100,
        TRUE ~ NA_real_
      ),
      reliability = case_when(
        is.na(cv) ~ "Unavailable",
        cv < 12 ~ "Reliable",
        cv <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
        TRUE ~ "Unreliable"
      )
    )
}

poverty_2010 <- calculate_rate(poverty_2010)
poverty_2017 <- calculate_rate(poverty_2017)

poverty_2017 %>%
  count(reliability)


# A tibble: 4 × 2
  reliability           n
  <chr>             <int>
1 Reliable             22
2 Somewhat reliable   332
3 Unavailable           8
4 Unreliable           22


The two periods contain 384 tracts each. In 2013–2017, 22 tract estimates are reliable under the CV rule, 332 are somewhat reliable, 22 are unreliable, and 8 have no calculable rate.


Show code
poverty_wide <- bind_rows(
  poverty_2010,
  poverty_2017
) %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, period, rate, rate_moe) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = period,
    values_from = c(rate, rate_moe)
  )

poverty_tested <- poverty_wide %>%
  mutate(
    change = `rate_2013-2017` - `rate_2006-2010`,
    se_1 = `rate_moe_2006-2010` / 1.645,
    se_2 = `rate_moe_2013-2017` / 1.645,
    se_diff = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
    moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,
    significant = abs(change) > moe_diff,
    change_pp = change * 100,
    moe_diff_pp = moe_diff * 100
  )

poverty_tested %>%
  count(significant)


# A tibble: 3 × 2
  significant     n
  <lgl>       <int>
1 FALSE         313
2 TRUE           63
3 NA              8


Of the 376 tracts with usable rates in both periods, 63 show a statistically detectable change at the 90% confidence level: 36 increased and 27 decreased. The other 313 do not show a detectable change. Eight tracts cannot be tested because their poverty-status population is zero in at least one period, making the rate undefined. I leave these eight in the data as missing values and exclude them only from calculations that require a rate.


Show code
poverty_2010 %>%
  summarize(zero_denominators = sum(totalE == 0))


# A tibble: 1 × 1
  zero_denominators
              <int>
1                 7


Show code
poverty_2017 %>%
  summarize(zero_denominators = sum(totalE == 0))


# A tibble: 1 × 1
  zero_denominators
              <int>
1                 8


Show code
poverty_tested %>%
  filter(!is.na(significant)) %>%
  summarize(
    detectable_increases = sum(significant & change > 0),
    detectable_decreases = sum(significant & change < 0)
  )


# A tibble: 1 × 2
  detectable_increases detectable_decreases
                 <int>                <int>
1                   36                   27



Changes and their uncertainty
The bars below show the 15 largest estimated increases. An error bar that crosses zero means that its change is not detectable at the 90% confidence level.


Show code
poverty_tested %>%
  filter(!is.na(significant)) %>%
  arrange(desc(change_pp)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15) %>%
  mutate(
    NAME = str_remove(
      NAME,
      ", Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania"
    )
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(NAME, change_pp), y = change_pp)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(
      ymin = change_pp - moe_diff_pp,
      ymax = change_pp + moe_diff_pp
    ),
    width = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Largest estimated increases in tract poverty rates",
    subtitle = "2006–2010 to 2013–2017 ACS; error bars show 90% MOE",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Change in poverty rate (percentage points)"
  )





Estimated poverty-rate changes and 90% margins of error for the 15 tracts with the largest estimated increases.






A second view of the changes
Each point below represents one tract. Color indicates whether its change is detectable at the 90% confidence level.


Show code
poverty_tested %>%
  filter(!is.na(significant)) %>%
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = `rate_2006-2010` * 100,
      y = change_pp,
      color = significant
    )
  ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Poverty changes vary across Philadelphia tracts",
    subtitle = "2006–2010 to 2013–2017 ACS",
    x = "2006–2010 poverty rate (%)",
    y = "Change (percentage points)",
    color = "Detectable change"
  )





Earlier poverty rate and later change for Philadelphia tracts with calculable rates in both periods.






Reliability table
This table shows five examples from each CV category. It is a sample of tracts, not the complete list.


Show code
reliability_table <- poverty_2017 %>%
  filter(!is.na(cv)) %>%
  arrange(desc(cv)) %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    dot = case_when(
      cv < 12 ~ "🟢",
      cv <= 40 ~ "🟡",
      TRUE ~ "🔴"
    ),
    NAME = str_remove(
      NAME,
      ", Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania"
    ),
    rate_pct = rate * 100,
    moe_pp = rate_moe * 100
  ) %>%
  select(dot, NAME, rate_pct, moe_pp, cv, reliability)

reliability_table %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(rate_pct, moe_pp, cv),
    decimals = 1
  ) %>%
  cols_label(
    dot = "",
    NAME = "Tract",
    rate_pct = "Poverty rate (%)",
    moe_pp = "Rate MOE (points)",
    cv = "CV (%)",
    reliability = "Reliability"
  ) %>%
  cols_align(align = "center", columns = dot) %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Reliability of tract poverty-rate estimates",
    subtitle = "Philadelphia, 2013–2017 ACS; five examples per category"
  ) %>%
  tab_source_note(
    "CV = (rate MOE / 1.645) / rate × 100. Jurjevich et al. (2018) thresholds: <12% reliable; 12–40% somewhat reliable; >40% unreliable."
  )

title: Verify the Claim: Option A
text:
Part 3 — Adjudicate
Supported. The article describes Philadelphia’s 2013–2017 poverty rate as approximately 26%. A separate ACS estimate for Philadelphia County is 25.8%, which rounds to 26%. The tract results also show that poverty rates increased detectably in some parts of the city: 36 tracts show an increase at the 90% confidence level.
Not supported by this test. A broad reading that poverty rose dramatically across Philadelphia as a whole goes further than these tract results show. Only 36 of 376 comparable tracts show a detectable increase; 27 show a detectable decrease, and 313 show no detectable change. This does not disprove an increase in any particular neighborhood. Cannot be determined: The article’s exact figures for Eastwick, Fairhill, and Holmesburg cannot be checked with this tract analysis because the article does not provide its tract-to-neighborhood boundaries. Its claim about white poverty also requires race-specific data, which the overall poverty variables here do not measure.


Show code
get_city_rate <- function(yr) {
  get_acs(
    geography = "county",
    variables = poverty_vars,
    state = "PA",
    county = "Philadelphia",
    year = yr,
    survey = "acs5",
    output = "wide"
  ) %>%
    mutate(
      period = paste0(yr - 4, "-", yr),
      rate = belowE / totalE,
      rate_moe = moe_prop(belowE, totalE, belowM, totalM)
    )
}

city_rates <- bind_rows(
  get_city_rate(2010),
  get_city_rate(2017)
)

city_rates %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate_pct = rate * 100,
    rate_moe_pp = rate_moe * 100
  ) %>%
  select(period, poverty_rate_pct, rate_moe_pp)


# A tibble: 2 × 3
  period    poverty_rate_pct rate_moe_pp
  <chr>                <dbl>       <dbl>
1 2006-2010             25.1       0.541
2 2013-2017             25.8       0.460

title: Verify the Claim: Option A
text:
Part 4 — Rewrite
Philadelphia’s 2013–2017 ACS puts the city’s poverty rate at about 26%. Across its census tracts, the pattern of change is mixed. Compared with 2006–2010, 36 tracts had a detectable increase in poverty rates, while 27 had a detectable decrease. In another 313 tracts, the estimated change was too uncertain to distinguish from zero at the 90% confidence level. These tract results cannot confirm the article’s precise figures for named neighborhoods, because the article does not identify which tracts it used to define them.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number published by the American Community Survey is an estimate based on a sample rather than a complete count. Each estimate therefore comes with a margin of error that describes its statistical uncertainty.
In this analysis, I examine median gross rent across counties in New York State and ask which communities are measured most and least reliably. Understanding the uncertainty in rent estimates is important because these data may influence housing policy and the allocation of affordable housing resources.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Choosing what to measure

my_state <- "NY"
my_variable <- "B25064_001"

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Pulling the data

county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = my_variable,
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)

Let’s look at what came back.

dim(county_data)

[1] 62  5

head(county_data)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  GEOID NAME                         variable   estimate   moe
  <chr> <chr>                        <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>
1 36001 Albany County, New York      B25064_001     1252    22
2 36003 Allegany County, New York    B25064_001      754    33
3 36005 Bronx County, New York       B25064_001     1436    11
4 36007 Broome County, New York      B25064_001      914    26
5 36009 Cattaraugus County, New York B25064_001      759    30
6 36011 Cayuga County, New York      B25064_001      895    39


The dataset contains 62 rows, with one observation for each county-level unit in New York State. This matches the 62 counties and county equivalents in the state.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 100 dollars means something different for an estimate of 800 dollars than for an estimate of 2,000 dollars. To compare uncertainty across counties, I calculate the margin of error as a percentage of the estimate.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

Now I sort the counties to identify the least reliable estimates.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                        estimate   moe moe_pct
   <chr>                          <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Hamilton County, New York        860    95   11.0 
 2 Schuyler County, New York        858    75    8.74
 3 Greene County, New York          993    79    7.96
 4 Lewis County, New York           821    59    7.19
 5 Orleans County, New York         877    60    6.84
 6 Yates County, New York           802    46    5.74
 7 Wyoming County, New York         782    44    5.63
 8 Cortland County, New York        911    50    5.49
 9 Chenango County, New York        819    44    5.37
10 Livingston County, New York      912    48    5.26


Hamilton County has the largest margin of error relative to its estimate. Its estimated median gross rent is 860 dollars, with a margin of error of 95 dollars. The margin of error is therefore approximately 11.0 percent of the estimate.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Sorting counties into reliability categories

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence    51
2 Low confidence      1
3 Moderate           10


Using these thresholds, 51 counties are classified as high confidence, 10 as moderate, and one as low confidence. These thresholds are analytical categories used to compare counties in this report rather than official Census Bureau standards.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To compare the reliability of the rent estimate with county population, I pull median gross rent and total population together in wide format.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                         myvarE myvarM    popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                         <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 36001 Albany County, New York        1252     22  315374    NA
2 36003 Allegany County, New York       754     33   47027    NA
3 36005 Bronx County, New York         1436     11 1419250    NA
4 36007 Broome County, New York         914     26  197738    NA
5 36009 Cattaraugus County, New York    759     30   76479    NA
6 36011 Cayuga County, New York         895     39   75464    NA


The E suffix identifies an estimate, while the M suffix identifies its margin of error. Therefore, myvarE and myvarM contain the median gross rent estimate and margin of error, while popE and popM contain the corresponding population values.

county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now I compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         51        381479.
2 Low confidence           1          5102 
3 Moderate                10         41178.


High-confidence counties have an average population of approximately 381,479, compared with approximately 41,178 in moderate-confidence counties. Hamilton County, the only low-confidence county, has an estimated population of 5,102. This pattern suggests that counties with smaller populations tend to have less precise median gross rent estimates. It is consistent with the smaller ACS samples generally available in less populated places.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
The results show that Hamilton County is the New York county we know the least about for median gross rent. Its estimated median gross rent is $860, with a margin of error of $95, or about 11.0 percent of the estimate. It is the only county classified as low confidence under the thresholds used here. Schuyler and Greene Counties also have relatively large margins of error, at approximately 8.7 percent and 8.0 percent, respectively, and are classified as moderate confidence.
This pattern is related to the way the American Community Survey works. The ACS is based on a sample rather than a complete count of every household. Counties with smaller populations generally provide fewer sampled households, so their estimates tend to be less precise. In this analysis, high-confidence counties have an average population of about 381,479, compared with about 41,178 for moderate-confidence counties and 5,102 for the low-confidence county. These results are consistent with the expectation that smaller places are measured with greater uncertainty.
Ignoring this uncertainty could create unfair policy outcomes. If New York State allocated affordable-housing funds using median rent estimates alone, Hamilton County could be treated as though its estimate were just as precise as estimates for much larger counties. A county near a funding threshold might receive too little assistance, or be excluded entirely, because of sampling variation rather than a genuine difference in housing needs. Agencies should therefore consider both the estimate and its margin of error, especially when making decisions about small rural communities.

Week 3 Notes
Ansombe’s Quartet Same: mean x,y, correlation, regression line
plot is a mapping from columns in your data to visual properties on your page. (“grammar of graphics”) “gg”
your data: page(canvas): estimate > position on the y-axis population > position on x-axis reliability > color moe > size
p < 1. ggplot(data)-data i’m using > create a blank canvas 2. aes(…) Aesthetic Mappings. no decorating 3. geom_*() the shape/type of chart
ggplot(tract_data) + aes(x=population, y=moe_pct) + geom_point()
inside aes(). Not inside aes(color=reliability). geom_point(“blue”) decorations
ggplot(county_data) + aes(x=estimate, y=population, (color=“blue”)x) + geom_point(color=“blue”)
what i want to know GEOM how a variable is spread. geom_histogram() how do two variables relate geom_point() how do groups compare. geom_boxplot() how do things change over time geom_line() how uncertain is a value. geom_error bar()
facet_wrap(~reliability)
Coefficient of Variation (CV) -relative measure of sampling error standard error/estimate * 100
Low CV: 15% > high reliability Medium: 15-30% High: 30% > high sampling error
Derived Uncertainty Pov. Rate = # in poverty +- moe / total pop +-moe moe_sum() > adding estimates together moe_pop() > one estimate as share a another moe_ratio() > pov#/HH income, one not a subset of another
Change over time 1. the overlapping intervals 2019-2023, 2018-2022 compare non-overlapping intervals 2014-2018 vs 2019-2023
The standard error of difference SEdiff = sqrt(SE1 ^2 + SE2 ^2) z = (est1 - est2)/SEdiff
Confidence Interval of Change Interval = Difference +- (1.645*SEdiff)
